title: PaNaBat: German-Chilean research project targets sustainable battery materials - electrive.com
content:
In Brief
The newly launched German-Chilean research project PaNaBat aims to strengthen cooperation in research and education, technology transfer and industrial collaboration for sustainable battery materials, lithium extraction and battery recycling.
The research project aims to establish a foundation for a sustainable circular economy in the European battery market. A key element of PaNaBat is the creation of an information and networking platform linking project partners, companies and research institutions.
In addition, PaNaBat focuses on developing a sustainable circular economy for battery materials such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and aluminium. The project covers advanced recycling processes with closed material loops and a low carbon footprint, as well as automated battery dismantling, new sorting technologies and efficient material recovery methods. Rather than recovering materials to their elemental form, the aim is to preserve their functional properties wherever possible so they can be reused directly in battery production. Another focus is assessing the environmental impact of new technologies.
The German Federal Ministry of Research is funding the PaNaBat project with €450,000. The project brings together Chile’s Universidad Católica del Norte, Fraunhofer Chile and the German Fraunhofer Institutes for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST, for Solar Energy Systems ISE and for Silicate Research ISC. Fraunhofer ISC is also responsible for coordinating the project.

title: Brookfield to acquire Aypa Power in $7bn battery storage deal – Batteries International
content: Brookfield Asset Management is to acquire US battery storage developer Aypa Power in a $7 billion enterprise value deal. Brookfield confirmed on July 22 that it had entered into an agreement to acquire Aypa from funds managed by Blackstone Energy Transition Partners for around $7 billion enterprise value at closing, or an equity value of $3 billion. Aypa has about 6.5GW of operating and contracted capacity and a >20GW development pipeline across the US and Canada. Under the terms of the deal, Brookfield will acquire Aypa’s operating, under-construction and contracted project portfolio, together with its development platform. Brookfield said the transaction, which is subject to various regulatory approvals, will give it a leading presence in the North American BESS market and help Aypa deliver on its next phase of growth. Bilal Khan, senior MD, and Mark Zhu, MD from Blackstone said: “We invested in Aypa based on our conviction that battery storage would become increasingly critical to supporting grid reliability and meeting growing electricity demand from AI and other use cases. “Since then, the company has established itself as the leading battery storage platform in North America, supported by a premier development pipeline and strong customer relationships.” Clarios, the world’s largest manufacturer of automotive batteries, is owned by Brookfield Business Partners together with institutional partners of Brookfield Asset Management. title: Italy's STC secures US orders for innovative lead refining system – Batteries International
content: Italian lead recycler and engineering firm STC has told Batteries International it has completed the shipment of two state-of-the-art refining systems to major secondary lead producers in the US. STC’s innovative Oxy-Air Lance systems have been shipped to two firms, although confidentiality agreements mean the two clients cannot be named. However, STC commercial and marketing director Alberto Bergamaschini said on July 28 the recent shipments and commissioning of the systems is a major coup for the company on the international market. Oxy-Air Lance offers intelligent oxygen injection technology for safer, more efficient lead refining. Bergamaschini said the system gives secondary lead producers higher refining consistency, lower maintenance costs and greater process reliability — marking what he claimed is a significant step forward compared with traditional, manually-operated systems. Each of the systems delivered to the US comprise a dual-line configuration, capable of independently supplying two submerged lances simultaneously, with completely independent control circuits, regulation systems and operating parameters for each lance. In secondary lead refining, the selective oxidation of antimony, arsenic and tin is one of the most critical metallurgical operations. “Process efficiency depends not only on the correct oxygen injection rate, but also on maintaining the refining kettle within a controlled temperature range throughout the operation,” Bergamaschini said. Unlike conventional oxy-lance systems available on the market, he said STC’s system can operate in two different modes: • Traditional manual operation, where the operator independently adjusts compressed air and oxygen flow rates through manual control valves; • Fully automated PLC-controlled operation, where a dedicated control system continuously regulates both oxygen and compressed air through precision control valves according to the process requirements. The automatic operating mode represents one of the most innovative features of the STC system, Bergamaschini said. Intelligent temperature control is another important benefit. During lead refining, oxygen reacts selectively with antimony, arsenic and part of the lead, producing lead-rich oxides that float to the bath surface and can subsequently be removed. As these oxidation reactions are strongly exothermic, excessive oxygen input can rapidly increase the bath temperature. In conventional, manually-operated systems, maintaining the correct balance between oxygen and compressed air depends entirely on the operator’s experience. Small errors in flow adjustment can generate significant temperature fluctuations, causing thermal stress to the refining kettle. However, Bergamaschini said STC’s system continuously monitors process parameters and automatically adjusts the oxygen/air mixture using dedicated proportional control valves, maintaining the molten lead temperature within the desired operating range, which is typically 580–620°C. This has a number of advantages, including stable refining conditions, improved metallurgical efficiency and more consistent refining quality from batch to batch. The system incorporates multiple advanced safety features and can be supplied in different configurations depending on refinery capacity and kettle dimensions. title: Coreshell hails ‘China-free’ LFP supply deal with South Korea’s L&F – Batteries International
content: US battery tech company Coreshell Technologies has agreed an eight-year LFP supply deal with South Korea’s L&F Corporation in a move to offer a “fully China-free” nattery materials option. Corsehell said on July 14 the cathode active materials supply agreement eliminates “the final risk” in the battery supply chain in terms of foreign entities of concern (FEOC) — giving defence suppliers, OEMs and energy storage customers a fully China-free option. Coreshell, which develops high-performance batteries that replace graphite with domestically sourced metallurgical silicon, said the agreement marks a pivotal step in onshoring one of the most critical sourcing bottlenecks in the battery supply chain. Coreshell said the deal gives it access to one of the largest non-Chinese sources of LFP, delivering a battery supply chain that is fully compliant with emerging US sourcing requirements. “As US policy increasingly restricts battery materials sourced from FEOCs, manufacturers are facing growing pressure to build FEOC-free supply chains. “Today, the overwhelming majority of LFP is produced in China, leaving battery manufacturers exposed to geopolitical disruption, changing trade policies, and volatile lead times.” Coreshell said its proprietary nanomaterials enable metallurgical-grade silicon, sourced in the US, to perform reliably in lithium ion battery cells, eliminating the structural degradation that has historically limited metallurgical-grade silicon at scale. Combined with L&F’s LFP cathode active materials, this is the only verified, full-cell compliant supply chain combination available at commercial scale, the company claimed. “This agreement completes what we’ve been building toward — a battery manufactured in the US that’s fully free of Chinese minerals and components from anode to cathode, and that meets the highest compliance standards available,” said Jonathan Tan, CEO of Coreshell. Batteries International reported analysis earlier in July that eight of the top 10 integrators worldwide are now headquartered in China as the country continues its dominance of the international battery storage market. Energy data analytics firm Wood Mackenzie said non-FEOC sourcing requirements in the US will start at 55% of project costs in 2026, rising to 75% by 2030, a trajectory that will significantly constrain the ability of Chinese manufacturers to supply into the US market. title: Mars Builds Resilient Mint Supply Chains In Europe
content:
Mars Builds Resilient Mint Supply Chains In Europe
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mars is introducing traceable menthol into its European supply chain via its Shubh Mint programme (Image source: Mars)
Mars’ Shubh Mint programme builds traceable menthol supply chains, boosts farmer incomes and embeds climate‑smart practices in India for European gum
Sustainable sourcing is the prioritisation of purchasing goods and services that help protect the environment, support social equity and have lower carbon footprints, and it is increasingly central to supply chain strategy.
Mars is applying this approach by bringing
sustainably sourced and traceable
natural menthol into its European chewing gum supply chain to cut emissions and support resilient agriculture.
This programme connects field‑level practices in India to manufacturing operations in Europe, showing how upstream interventions can stabilise downstream production.
Our Sustainable in a Generation Plan
Mint as a critical ingredient in global chains
Mars is introducing traceable menthol into its European supply chain via its Shubh Mint programme so it can integrate sustainably sourced ingredients into its British and Polish
manufacturing operations
According to the company, “mint is a critical ingredient for many of Mars, Incorporated’s global brands,” which makes supply continuity and quality a core supply chain concern.
However, the current natural menthol supply chain is exposed to significant risk, as approximately 80% of the world’s natural menthol originates from Uttar Pradesh, India, concentrating production in one vulnerable geography.
Uttar Pradesh is known to experience climate change impacts, declining yields and rising production costs, which can undermine both farmer incomes and global supply security.
Synthetic menthol is widely used across the industry as an alternative, but Mars has been adamant about choosing natural mint because of its long‑term benefits for businesses,
farmers and resilient agriculture
, even though this requires deeper supply chain engagement.
Key Facts: Shubh Mint Supply Chain
Around 80% of the world’s natural menthol is produced in Uttar Pradesh, India.
Shubh Mint has engaged more than 24,000 farmers in climate‑smart mint production.
Farmers in the programme have seen mint incomes more than double.
More than 8,500 women have been trained in climate‑smart agriculture.
Smart practices have cut mint production costs by 20% while raising yields.
Meenal Bahirwani, Sustainable Sourcing Lead, Mars Snacking
Partnering to strengthen upstream supply chains
Tanager is a nonprofit organisation, affiliated with ACDI/VOCA, that specialises in supporting sustainable supply chains and was brought in as a partner when Mars launched Shubh Mint in 2017.
The initiative aims to strengthen natural mint production by increasing climate change resilience, improving farming practices and
supporting sustainable livelihoods
across mint‑growing communities that feed into Mars’ supply chain.
“Before the programme started, many mint farming households were struggling to remain profitable,” says Joseph Boulier, Managing Director of Food Systems at Tanager.
“Through Mars’ investment, farmers now have access to the knowledge, practices and inputs that have significantly improved their profitability.
“You can really see the difference in how the programme has impacted these mint farming communities.”
The mint programme began with a two‑year research and pilot phase so both organisations could better understand what was affecting farmer incomes and productivity, providing a data‑driven basis for supply chain interventions.
Climate‑smart agricultural practices and improved planting materials were trialled on quarter‑acre demonstration plots with volunteer farmers, enabling peer‑to‑peer learning, reducing the risks associated with adopting new techniques and building confidence before scaling the programme.
Mars' Shubh Programme has now engaged more than 24,000 farmers in India. Credit: Mars
Scaling resilient supply chains and women’s participation
Because the demonstration plots succeeded, the programme expanded into a full community‑wide initiative that now involves:
Increased farmer participation.
Building supply chains through Farmer Producer Companies.
Opportunities for women via Self‑Help Groups.
The programme has engaged more than 24,000 farmers, who have seen their incomes more than double from mint, supporting more stable and attractive participation in the supply chain.
More than 8,500 women are now trained in climate‑smart agricultural practices to support farming as a family business, adding capacity and knowledge within farming households that supply Mars.
More than 1,000 of these women have established their own independent income‑generating businesses, and more than 4,500 women have taken part in self‑help groups that provide financial literacy and confidence support, which helps diversify and stabilise household income.
“The most meaningful impact of Shubh is seeing women who once identified themselves with a thumbprint now proudly signing their own names," says Meenal Bahirwani, Sustainable Sourcing Lead, Mars Snacking.
“That simple change reflects something far greater: confidence, agency and the belief that they can shape their own futures.
“When women thrive, the impact extends far beyond them, strengthening families, inspiring communities and creating opportunities for the next generation.”
Mint is a specialty crop grown in the United States, Canada and India providing livelihoods to more than 1 million farmers. Credit: Mars
Climate‑smart practices and supply chain performance
Smart climate agricultural practices such as improved plant spacing, irrigation systems, intercropping and fertiliser management cut mint production costs by 20%, while improving yield and production, making the upstream supply chain more efficient and resilient.
Lower production costs and higher yields help farmers manage
climate and market volatility
, while giving Mars a more reliable, traceable source of natural menthol.
What began as a response to a single, vulnerable ingredient has become a long‑term commitment and a replicable blueprint for transforming agricultural systems and empowering communities.
Sam de Frates, VP Commercial and Sustainability, Mars Snacking Europe and Central Eurasia
This investment in people and the planet directly enabled the creation of a supply chain that is now strong enough for Mars to integrate the Shubh Mint source into commercial operations.
Mars is now systematically embedding Shubh Mint across its entire brand portfolio, linking product formulation to verified,
resilient sourcing streams
Towards responsible, year‑round supply chains
The Shubh Mint programme continues to expand, and Mars is now evolving Shubh Mint towards a "full farm" approach that helps support more farmers to achieve a verified living income across all crops, not just mint.
“What began as a response to a single, vulnerable ingredient has become a long‑term commitment and a replicable blueprint for transforming agricultural systems and empowering communities,” says Sam de Frates, VP Commercial and Sustainability, Mars Snacking Europe and Central Eurasia.
Sam de Frates, VP Commercial and Sustainability, Mars Snacking Europe and Central Eurasia
“The Mars Shubh Mint programme shows how sustainability and business performance go hand in hand.
"By investing in livelihoods and reducing environmental impact, we can build a more resilient and efficient supply chain."

title: Adecco & Achilles Data Exposes AI Gaps in Supply Chain
content:
Adecco & Achilles Data Exposes AI Gaps in Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Workforce data from the Adecco Group makes the operational friction between technology adoption and workforce execution clear. (Credit: The Adecco Group)
New research from Adecco and Achilles highlights the struggle to scale AI value ahead of Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in London, UK this September
AI is now embedded into global supply chain operations as our operations transform into a new digital phase. Insights from Achilles and The Adecco Group have found that significant investment in AI is now being met with calls for measurable operational returns.
Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index reveals US private AI investment reached US$285.9bn in 2025, growing 127.5% year over year. However, McKinsey reports that while 88% of organisations use AI in at least one function, only 39% have seen an enterprise-level EBIT impact.
These figures show the widening gap between investment and value, which highlights to logistics leaders that technology capability alone cannot fix fragmented operations.
This challenge, along with others surrounding AI implementation, will be part of leading discussions at S
upply Chain LIVE: The London Summit
, hosted by Supply Chain Digital and BizClik on 8 and 9 September 2026 at the QEII Centre in Westminster, London, UK.
Shifting from model access to operational value
Supply chain leaders who are trying to move past the initial phases of AI basics are now looking at shifting from acquiring large language models to re-engineering physical workflows.
The winners will not simply be the companies with access to the largest models or biggest compute budgets.
Lu Zhang, Founder and Managing Partner, Fusion Fund
However, this digital ecosystem is demanding financial discipline; infrastructure costs are high and buyers now expect to see a clear ROI across industrial automation and logistics networks.
“The winners will not simply be the companies with access to the largest models or biggest compute budgets,” says Lu Zhang, Founder and Managing Partner of Fusion Fund.
Lu Zhang, Founder and Managing Partner of Fusion Fund (Image source: Fusion Fund)
“They will be the companies that can turn AI into measurable workflow change, proprietary data advantage and real-world deployment.”
Those organisations unable to align algorithms with operational processes could see their supply chains vulnerable to scaled errors, as well as wasted capital.
Validating supplier data and closing risk gaps
Data from Achilles shows that more than a third (37%) of organisations currently either pilot or use
AI tools within procurement
and supplier risk management. Despite this, only 2% have fully integrated these platforms across their operational networks.
Not only this but most supply chains lack visibility beyond their Tier 1 suppliers, with Achilles research finding that only 6% maintain multi-tier oversight.
AI delivers value in supplier risk management only when it sits on trusted data, clear governance and the ability to fit into existing procurement processes.
Paul Guenther, Regional Director at Achilles
Supply chain leaders need to be cautious because if your supplier data is missing details or out of date, using
automated AI tools
won't fix the problem and instead is likely to make your mistakes bigger, faster and more difficult to catch.
“AI delivers value in supplier risk management only when it sits on trusted data, clear governance and the ability to fit into existing procurement processes,” Paul Guenther, Regional Director at Achilles, says. “If the foundations are wrong, AI simply scales the problem.”
Achilles research found 94% of supply chains lack visibility beyond their Tier 1 suppliers (Credit: Achilles)
Orchestrating the emerging hybrid workforce
Workforce data from the Adecco Group makes the operational friction between
technology adoption
and workforce execution clear.
The intelligent AI services market in logistics is projected to grow from US$24bn in 2024 to over US$740bn by 2034, driving a 37% shift in core supply chain job skills by 2030.
Yet, Adecco’s research reveals only 2% of logistics companies qualify as 'future-ready' based on leadership skills, upskilling investment and career mobility:
Leadership deficit: 51% of logistics executives state their leadership team is unprepared to leverage AI tools in decision-making, while 23% operate with no formal AI policy.
Employee misalignment: While 77% of logistics workers are comfortable collaborating with AI agents and 81% believe AI creates jobs, only 27% have been involved by employers in redesigning their roles.
Training gaps: Workers save an average of 2 hours per day using AI, but 42% of organisations deliver no formal AI reskilling, and only 35% of workers can measure the impact of their output.
Operational risk: 55% of logistics firms report AI has altered required role skills, yet 34% expect employees to adapt without structured support.
"As AI becomes more deeply embedded across the logistics industry, jobs are evolving," says Niki Turner-Harding, Senior Vice President & Country Head, Adecco UK & Ireland.
"The impact is being felt most visibly on the warehouse floor, where manual tasks are increasingly being augmented by technology and demand is growing for new skills and more technology-enabled roles. The good news is that workers are ready for that change.
Niki Turner-Harding, Senior Vice President & Country Head, Adecco UK & Ireland
"Our latest sectorial research found that 77% of employees would be comfortable collaborating with AI as part of their job. Yet only 27% say they have been actively involved in conversations about how
AI is reshaping their work
"The real opportunity for employers is to close that gap. The companies that will retain a competitive advantage will be those that invest not only in technology, but in helping their people adapt, develop new skills and become active participants in the transformation."
Forecasting AI at Supply Chain LIVE
How to align the use of AI with predictive analytics and worker safety, as well as continuous risk monitoring, will be just some of the key topics discussed during Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September 2026.
The event will convene more than 1,000 international supply chain, procurement and logistics executives to talk about what the next phase of enterprise automation could look like in reality.
A featured panel session,
The Future of AI in Supply Chain
, takes place on 9 September 2026 from 2:15pm to 3:00pm BST on the Supply Chain Stage.
Panellists, including executives from Diageo, ofi, and Amazon, will discuss predictive analytics, circular logistics and automated disruption resolution, sharing clear strategies for scaling AI sustainably.

title: NHTSA probes 1.2M Tesla Model 3, Model Y over suspension failures
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 31 2026 - 8:57 am PT
The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened an investigation into roughly 1.2 million Tesla vehicles after receiving 156 complaints of a front suspension component detaching while driving.
The probe covers 2018-2020 Model 3 and 2021-2023 Model Y vehicles, and it centers on the front lower lateral link separating from the car.
What NHTSA is looking at
The agency’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) opened a preliminary evaluation, the first stage of its process. If ODI finds a safety-related defect, it can escalate to an engineering analysis and, eventually, force a recall.
According to the investigation documents, the front lower lateral link has detached in the affected cars. That’s a core piece of the front suspension. When it lets go, the agency says the vehicle can lose steering control, become undriveable, and need to be towed.
The complaint pattern is the part that stands out. Most owners reported no advance warning before the link failed. Some said they heard noises beforehand, but many didn’t get even that. A suspension component that separates without warning is a very different safety picture than one that clunks and rattles for weeks first.
For now, NHTSA says it isn’t aware of any crashes, injuries, or fatalities tied to the defect. That’s good news, but 156 complaints is not a small number for a preliminary evaluation.
This isn’t Tesla’s first suspension problem
Tesla has been down this road before with the same part on the same cars.
The company issued a
recall in 2021 covering roughly 2,800 Model 3 vehicles
over a suspension issue tied to a production problem. A second recall in 2023 hit 422 Model 3 vehicles for similar failures. NHTSA says the failures it’s now investigating go beyond the scope of those earlier recalls, and they don’t appear to be the same production issue.
Suspension has been a recurring headache for Tesla with regulators. Back in 2020,
Tesla came under NHTSA scrutiny over Model S and Model X suspension
after it disputed a related recall in China. That saga stretched on for years before the agency closed it in 2024 without forcing a recall, though it did recommend Tesla change a part.
The pattern is a familiar one: complaints pile up, Tesla points to isolated causes, and NHTSA has to decide whether there’s a systemic defect underneath.
Where this sits with Tesla’s other open probes
The suspension probe lands while Tesla is already dealing with heavier NHTSA scrutiny elsewhere. The agency
upgraded its investigation into Full Self-Driving over reduced-visibility crashes to cover 3.2 million vehicles
earlier this year, moving that case one step closer to a possible recall.
Electrek’s Take
A part that holds the front wheel to the car shouldn’t fall off, and it definitely shouldn’t fall off without warning. The good news is that no one has been hurt yet, or at least that NHTSA knows of, and a lateral link failure at low speed is survivable in a way a lot of other suspension failures aren’t. But “no injuries yet” is exactly the window regulators are supposed to act in.
A preliminary evaluation is early. It could close with nothing, like the Model S/X case did. But 156 complaints and a no-warning failure mode is the kind of combination that tends to get upgraded, not dropped. We’ll be watching whether ODI escalates this to an engineering analysis, which is the real tell that a recall is coming.

title: HMP’s new $3,999 electric scooter is the affordable, street-legal commuter the US needs
content:
Electric Motorcycles
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Jul 31 2026 - 8:24 am PT
The US electric two-wheeler market has no shortage of high-powered electric motorcycles and moped-style e-bikes. But if you’re looking for something in between – a practical, street-legal electric scooter built for everyday transportation rather than weekend thrills – your options are surprisingly limited.
That’s why the new HMP Lightning MK.II caught my attention.
After recently covering
the company’s flagship Flash electric scooter
, which offers a blistering 75 mph (120 km/h) top speed, HMP is now introducing a more approachable model that feels better suited to the needs of most riders. The new Lightning MK.II tops out at 56 mph (90 km/h), costs just
US $3,999
, and is designed specifically for commuting, errands, and even delivery work.
For many riders, that combination may actually make it the more compelling option.
The Lightning MK.II is classified as a DOT-approved motorcycle, meaning it can be registered, plated, and insured for road use. In some states like California, that also means riders can legally take advantage of lane splitting, one of the biggest benefits of commuting on two wheels.
Power comes from a swingarm-mounted electric motor producing 4,000W of continuous power and up to 7,000W peak, pushing the scooter to its 56 mph (90 km/h) top speed. That’s paired with a removable 74V 45Ah (3.33 kWh) lithium battery that offers up to 62 miles (100 km) of range under ideal conditions. Plus, even with that huge battery, there’s still more storage room underneath the seat.
Like many modern electric scooters, the battery can be removed for charging indoors, eliminating one of the biggest hurdles for apartment dwellers or anyone without access to outdoor charging.
The included 120V charger fills the pack in around 4.5 hours, making overnight charging simple, or even topping up at work. Hey, it may only cost $0.50 to charge up, but why not let your employer pay for your ‘fuel’?
The scooter is also designed with practicality in mind. It seats two riders, supports up to 397 lb (180 kg), and includes a rack-ready rear end for cargo or delivery accessories. HMP also opted for a side-mounted motor and single-sided swingarm, making rear tire and brake maintenance significantly easier than on many traditional scooters.
One thing I particularly like is that HMP ships the scooter fully assembled. Unlike many lower-cost electric motorcycles and scooters that require varying degrees of setup after delivery, the Lightning MK.II arrives ready to ride.
While 56 mph (90 km/h) might sound modest compared to the ever-growing crop of high-speed electric motorcycles, it’s worth remembering that this is already enough performance for the vast majority of urban riding.
In fact, my wife and I have relied on a nearly identical performance Gogoro electric scooter as our only “big” vehicle for years. We do almost everything else on e-bikes, but whenever we need to travel farther to neighboring cities or suburbs, carry more, or simply keep up with faster city traffic, the scooter gets the job done. It comfortably carries both of us, handles grocery runs with ease, and has proven that scooter life can absolutely replace a car for many urban households. So I’m already sold on the scooter lifestyle and can tell you that a bike like the Lightning MK.II is probably enough for the vast majority of urban residents out there.
And that’s one reason I’m always excited to see more companies bringing practical electric scooters to the US market.
Unlike Europe or much of Asia, where electric scooters have become a common sight, American buyers still have remarkably few options. The market tends to jump straight from e-bikes to more expensive and powerful electric motorcycles, leaving a noticeable gap for affordable, approachable urban transportation. And that’s not even mentioning the added utility that step-through seated scooters offer compared to full-on electric motorcycles.
At $3,999, the HMP Lightning MK.II helps fill that gap in the market. It offers enough speed for real-world commuting, removable battery convenience, room for two riders, and pricing that’s thousands less than many electric motorcycles.
If more companies start building electric scooters like this, I think we’ll finally begin seeing the kind of practical electric transportation that’s already transforming cities elsewhere in the world. And for riders looking for a genuine car alternative rather than just another recreational toy, that’s very good news indeed!

title: Hyundai IONIQ 5 spotted with a new high-tech setup and large 18" digital screen
content:
Hyundai IONIQ 5
Peter Johnson
| Jul 31 2026 - 7:16 am PT
A mysterious
test mule was caught in South Korea with an all-new interior setup, including a large 18″ infotainment screen.
When is Hyundai launching its first SDV?
Hyundai Motor Group is betting heavily on software and AI to drive growth over the next few years as it aims to become a “software-centric mobility leader.”
Pleos Connect infotainment system
and OS are at the heart of it all. Based on the Android Automotive OS, Hyundai’s Pleos’s new system is similar to what’s found in Tesla models, with apps and customizable screens like a smartphone.
The Grandeur was the first to launch in Korea with the new infotainment system earlier this year, while the IONIQ 3 is Hyundai’s first European model to offer the high-tech new setup.
The system is the “first tangible step” toward an SDV (Software Defined Vehicle) architecture, which will enable new in-car features, autonomous driving, and a personalized driving experience.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior with Pleos Connect infotainment system (Source: Hyundai)
Hyundai plans to launch its first SDV in 2027, and it appears the IONIQ 5 could be among the first to receive the upgrade.
An IONIQ 5 prototype was spotted in South Korea with a completely new high-tech setup. The images from
JHS_car.x
TheKoreanCarBlog
) reveal a minimalist design with one large 17″ or 18″ central infotainment screen.

Will Hyundai launch the IONIQ 5 as its first SDV? It has yet to be confirmed. The prototype could also be a mid-cycle refresh or update. However, as Hyundai’s most popular electric vehicle, it may make sense.

title: Anyland Rev Pro e-motos have this one weird trick...auto wheelies!
content:
Seth Weintraub
| Jul 31 2026 - 5:55 am PT
We’ve seen quite a few
low-cost
e-Moto pit bikes
that flirt with the $1000 price tag over the past months, but today’s has a really interesting trick: It auto-wheelies. It can’t be that simple can it? I grabbed my 14-year-old and some extra padding to find out.
At first glance, the Anyland Rev Pro looks similar, though admittedly more refined, to your garden variety Tuttio/
HeyBike Villan
mini pit bike.
The spec sheet will look familiar:
3,000W peak mid-drive, 160 Nm peak torque
Top speed:
34 mph (55 km/h), with 12 and 22 mph limited modes
Battery:
48V 22.5Ah (1,080 Wh) lithium-ion
Claimed range:
Up to 48 miles
Charge time:
5-5.5 hours with included 54.6V 4.5A fast charger
116 lb (52.6 kg)
Max load:
Hydraulic disc, front and rear
Suspension:
Inverted hydraulic fork, adjustable rear shock
14″/12″ puncture-resistant
2.6″ color LCD, LED headlight, IPX5 water resistance
$1,399 (from a $1,799 MSRP, with some colorways dipping to $1,299)
$100 off with code
Electrek
You’ve got the same mini Sur Ron look, similar 14/12 mullet tire setup, similar 1kWh battery, 3kW motor. Suspension is an inverted hydraulic fork up front with an adjustable rear shock, and braking comes from hydraulic discs at both ends with thick moto-style pads – appropriate hardware for a bike that will spend much of its life with the front wheel in the air and thus braking heavily on the rear. Most people at the rideout are going to just assume you’ve got a fancy Yozma IN10.
But Anyland Rev Pro isn’t just a Yozma with a fast charger and an interesting name. The controller was built with a company called Moxin which is all the rage with the Sur Ron wheelie crowd these days. Moxin controllers typically cost around
$1000 BY ITSELF
so putting something similar in a $1300 e-moto is certainly a noteworthy trick.
Now, Anyland’s bike doesn’t have an actual Moxin controller. The team there says that they worked with Moxin and calls their controller…
The WELIXON™ Wheelie-Assist Control System
brings auto-wheelie assist, gyro-based stability, and real-time angle monitoring to help new riders practice with more control and confidence.
Co-designed with Moxin
, an industry leader in auto-wheelie controller technology, it gives beginners a smarter way to build skills and gives parents greater peace of mind.
The controller co-designed with Moxin and fine-tuned specifically for the Rev Pro’s motor, battery output, throttle behavior, frame balance, and riding setup. That tuning helps improve compatibility, stabilize power delivery, and make wheelie assist feel more predictable.
As someone who left chunks of my knees and elbows on the El Segundo streets testing a more powerful-than-it-looks Talaria MX-4 a few years ago, I’m particularly uncomfortable with “looping out” as the kids say. So that’s where I throw my 14-year-old offspring at this job and justify his “salary” and Roth IRA.
The way it works is refreshingly simple. You pick one of three preset wheelie angles – 25°, 35°, or 45° – bounce the front and then pin the throttle. The bike’s IMU monitors your pitch in real time, modulating motor output to lift the front wheel and hold it at your chosen angle. The system is essentially doing the throttle-finesse part of a wheelie for you, which is exactly the part that sends beginners (like me!) looping out onto their backs.
That leaves you free to work on the part electronics can’t do for you: side-to-side balance. And that’s why I’d push back on anyone dismissing this as a toy. It’s closer to training wheels in the best sense – a progression tool. Start at 25°, work your way up, and when you’ve built the muscle memory, switch the assist off entirely and the Rev Pro behaves like any other throttle-controlled electric dirt bike for practicing manual wheelies.
How did it work?
Really quickly. My son and his friend, who already wheelie on BMX and mountain bikes but were afraid to on e-Motos, took to the 25-degree angle pretty quickly, even though that “didn’t feel natural at all”.
Then, after 10 minutes at 25 degrees, moved to 35 degrees, which “felt way more natural”. But the devil is in the details here. While the controller won’t let you loop out, it doesn’t help with the left and right balance and steering of the wheelie, and that’s what takes some training.
Then the very iconic 45-degree wheelie.
Today, they are now learning to wheelie on other e-Bikes but with this experience have skipped most of the lopping and leaving skin on the road.
Is a wheelie machine a bit ridiculous? Sure. But learning wheelies the traditional way involves a lot of falling, and falling is the number one reason people give up on it. If a controller can compress that learning curve while keeping riders off the pavement, that’s a legitimate safety story wearing a party hat.
Also it should be noted that Anyland threw in some nice perks besides the wheelies. The look of the bike is more refined than a Tuttio, and the waterproofing is nice. The 4.5A charger is much nicer, quieter, and obviously twice as fast at charging as the 2A chargers you will typically find with these more generic bikes (and also you will find with Anyland’s $899 variety). Also for shis-and-giggles, Anyland included a front lighting system that not only does a yellow and white light for nighttime but also includes a red-and-blue flashing light that mimics the local cops that will be confiscating your bike if you ride these on public roads.
Electrek’s Take
The mini electric dirt bike segment has a differentiation problem – dozens of brands selling nearly identical hardware on thinner and thinner margins. Anyland’s answer is the smartest kind: don’t race to the bottom on price, add a feature people actually want and can’t get elsewhere at this price point.
And the wheelie assist is that feature. Moxin’s anti-loop controllers have already proven themselves in the aftermarket, where riders pay a hefty premium to retrofit them. Getting that tech factory-integrated on a $1,300 bike with respectable-for-the-class components is a legitimately good deal, and it makes the Rev Pro an easy recommendation for its target rider: the beginner or teen who wants to learn wheelies without donating skin to the pavement gods.
If you have zero interest in wheelies, the calculus changes – there are comparable bikes at or below this price, including Anyland’s own $899 Rev 01, which shares the same motor, battery, and top speed while skipping the party trick and the fast charger. But then again, if you have zero interest in wheelies, I’m not sure why you’re shopping for a 116 lb electric dirt bike in the first place.
The Rev Pro knows exactly what it is: a fun machine with a genuinely novel trick that doubles as a safety feature. In a segment full of clones, that counts for a lot.

title: UK solar capacity hits 22.8 GW as market prepares for plug-in launch - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The UK added over 2 GW of solar capacity in the 12 months to the end of June 2026. With new plug-in solar regulations soon to take effect, a UK wholesaler boss tells
pv magazine
plug-in solar is a great opportunity to further grow the market.
Matthew Lynas
31 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Residential
Utility-scale
Image – Wikimedia Commons
There were 27,391 new UK solar installations in June 2026, the second highest monthly installations volume on record, adding 132 MW of capacity. Total UK solar capacity reached 22.8 GW by the end of June, according to the latest government deployment data.
March 2026 remains the strongest month for number of installations with 28,782 recorded, although solar deployment statistics from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) are provisional and subject to revision. DESNZ recorded a total of 2,076,000 UK solar installations at the end of June.
The barrier for entry to the distributed solar market will be lowered when new regulations on plug-in solar come into force on August 27, potentially opening up opportunities in the rental sector. Updated regulations will allow households to self-install systems up to an 800 W limit per electrical circuit.
Major retailers
have been in consultation with the UK government ahead of the launch, while product manufacturers are currently planning launch events timed for the regulation change.
Segen UK & Ireland managing director
David Hope
pv magazine
the UK wholesaler views plug-in solar as an additional market, rather than a cannibalization risk.
“We don’t think it’s a threat to rooftops, we think it’s a good product range with a couple of caveats. We need to make sure that the manufacturers are tier-one manufacturers,” said Hope, adding that the wholesaler would want to see products installed by qualified electricians.
“But take away those caveats and it’s a great opportunity to grow the market even further. So hopefully exciting times ahead,” he said.
More utility-scale plants are also in the pipeline. UK solar capacity increased 2.2 GW (10.9%) in the 12 months to the end of June 2026 and new capacity included the the largest operational UK solar farm to date – the 373 MW
Cleve Hill
solar farm.
Even larger projects are in active development following recent contracts for difference (CfD) tender rounds, which procured a record amount of solar capacity. The UK government secured 4.9 GW of capacity in its
seventh (AR7) CfD
allocation round, with 1.87 GW expected to come online by 2028 and 3 GW expected in 2029. The application window for AR8 will close on Aug. 7, 2026.

title: Solar's share of EU electricity demand tops 20% for three consecutive months - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Data compiled by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE shows photovoltaics supplied more than 20% of EU electricity demand in May, June and July for the first time. Latvia set a new EU record, with solar meeting 49% of the country’s electricity demand in June.
Sandra Enkhardt
31 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Image: Unsplash
Solar’s share of electricity demand across the 27 EU member states exceeded 20% for the first time for three consecutive months, according to data from the Energy-Charts platform compiled by Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE.
Energy-Charts calculated a share of 20.3% for May, 21.1% for June and 21.5% for July. As July has not yet fully ended, there may still be marginal changes, but the analysts say this will not affect the record.
During the same period last year, solar’s share of EU electricity demand ranged between 17.3% and 18.8%.
Records for Germany, Switzerland, Austria
Country-level data reveals a series of new records. In Germany, the solar share of electricity demand exceeded 30% for the first time and remained above this level for three consecutive months. Fraunhofer researchers recorded a share of 30.3% in May, 30.4% in June and a preliminary 31.6% in July. July marks a significant increase compared with the previous year, when weather conditions limited photovoltaics to a 22.6% share of electricity demand.
In Switzerland, the 25% threshold was exceeded and maintained for the first time over a three-month period. Energy-Charts reported a solar share of 25.8% in May, 25.3% in June and 26.5% in July. During the same months last year, solar accounted for between 19.1% and 21.8% of electricity demand.
Austria also set new records, achieving a record photovoltaic share of 23.3% of electricity demand in May. In June, the figure was 22.5%, while Energy-Charts reported 21.9% for July. All three values exceeded the previous record of 20.3% set in June 2025, which was the first time Austria surpassed the 20% threshold.
Baltic states lead EU solar shares
Latvia posted the highest solar share recorded in the EU, with photovoltaics accounting for 49% of electricity demand in June. Its Baltic neighbours, Lithuania and Estonia, also recorded strong figures, reaching 44.7% and 35.8%, respectively, in June.
The increase in Latvia is particularly striking. The country’s solar share was already 34.9% in April and rose to 40% in May. For July, Energy-Charts expects the figure to reach 38.9%. By comparison, values during the same period last year ranged between 13.7% and 18.9%.
High shares in Spain, Greece, Bulgaria
In Spain, the photovoltaic share of electricity demand remained consistently above 35% for the first time over the three-month period. The highest value was recorded in June, when solar accounted for 36.9% of electricity demand. Solar’s share was more than five percentage points higher than during the same period last year.
Similar figures were seen in Greece, where the solar share remained above 35% from May to July, representing an increase of more than seven percentage points compared with the same period last year.
In Bulgaria, meanwhile, solar shares – like in Germany – also exceeded 30% between May and July.
France, Italy remain below EU average
France also posted gains, continuing a rise of around two percentage points compared with the same periods in the previous year. However, the figures remain below EU averages. Solar reached its highest-ever share of electricity demand in July, at 14.6%. In June, the figure was 13.6%, while in May it was 12.6%, matching the previous record set in July 2025.
Like France, Italy also remained below the EU average. According to Energy-Charts data, Italy recorded its highest-ever solar share of electricity demand in May, at 19.5%. In July, however, the figure fell to just 16.7%, while June reached 18.5%.

title: Sierra Leone switches on solar-storage project - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Chinese manufacturer Sungrow, which commissioned the project, says its the country’s first national-scale power generation project connected to the grid in nearly a decade.
Patrick Jowett
31 Jul 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Sungrow
Chinese manufacturer Sungrow has commissioned a large-scale solar-plus-storage project in Sierra Leone.
According to an update from the company, the project is the first national-scale power generation project connected to the country’s grid in nearly a decade.
The World Bank-backed project features a solar array, of an undisclosed capacity, tied to 35 MWh energy storage system that integrates eight units of Sungrow’s
PowerTitan
Series ESS.
Sierra Leone has one of the lowest electricity access rates globally, with around 90% of those with access located in the capital, Freetown, and only five of the 16 regional capitals receiving partial electricity supply from diesel generators and hydropower facilities. The national grid records daily power outages of up to 18 hours.
Sungrow leveraged its PowerTitan’s black start and independent off-grid capabilities to implement an emergency response strategy during project implementation.
“Through the system’s black start capability, it can automatically switch to black start mode and establish a microgrid without external grid support, using solar power to support onsite loads and create a stable electrical environment for commissioning,” a statement from the company explains.
The project forms part of the Sierra Leone government’s Regional Emergency Solar Power Intervention Project, or RESPITE, a World Bank initiative aiming to increase the country’s national electricity access rate from 16% to 36%. Details on the government’s website add the project saw the inauguration of two solar projects – the 30 MW Newton solar power plant and 10 MW Lungi solar power plant – in June.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has identified 364 MW of operational solar in Sierra Leone, according to figures in its online project database, the majority of which is unidentified projects in the commercial and industrial market. It says a further 62 MW of solar are under construction.
AFSIA’s database adds that 28 MWh of battery storage is operational in the country, with a further 18.4 MWh under construction.

title: Europe's heatwave brings high irradiance as smoke, dust impact southern PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for pv magazine, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that Europe’s July heatwave led to positive irradiance anomalies across western and northern Europe, while wildfires in France and Spain and Saharan dust outbreaks increased the risk of panel soiling in the south of the continent.
31 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Image: Solcast
Europe’s July heatwave accompanied unusually high solar irradiance across much of western Europe, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Persistent high pressure limited cloud formation across the west and north of the continent, lifting irradiance well above typical July levels. At the same time, wildfires in France and Spain, together with Saharan dust outbreaks across the Mediterranean, added aerosols to the atmosphere and increased the risk of panel soiling.
The strongest positive irradiance anomalies were recorded across western and northern Europe, where cloud cover was suppressed for much of the month. Southern England, Wales and Ireland saw irradiance up to 35% above usual July levels, while northern France, the Low Countries and western Germany were up by around 25%. Southern Norway and Sweden were around 15% above usual. These conditions were linked to the same slow moving high-pressure systems that drove the month’s extreme heat. High pressure tends to stabilise the lower atmosphere and reduce cloud development. However, the continued high temperatures from June into July will have reduced PV module efficiency, partly offsetting the benefit of higher irradiance.
Across southern Europe, wildfire smoke and Saharan dust reduced the benefit of otherwise clear, high-irradiance summer conditions. Smoke from these fires reduced clear-sky irradiance across parts of southern France and Spain, with some smoke also spreading into neighbouring areas. Saharan dust outbreaks also crossed the Mediterranean at times, adding haze across parts of Spain, Italy and Greece. In southern Spain, where July irradiance is normally high at around 8.1 kWh/m² per day, monthly irradiance fell by as much as 4% to around 7.7 kWh/m², with larger reductions during individual smoke or dust events.
Aerosols also created a soiling risk where particles settled on PV modules and were not removed by rain or cleaning. Using PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations in the HSU soiling loss model, the end-of-month soiling impact for uncleaned panels was estimated at 5.6% in Valencia. This reflected both smoke from the nearby Vall d’Uixo wildfire and repeated Saharan dust episodes, with no appreciable rainfall events to clean panels during the month. Madrid saw a lower estimated impact of 2.2%, where nearby fire impacts were less prolonged and Saharan dust was less significant. In Bordeaux, nearby wildfires brought intense smoke pollution late in July, but rainfall events limited the estimated soiling impact to a peak of 0.6%.
The site-level soiling estimates show how similar regional aerosol conditions translated into different operational risks depending on local particulate exposure and whether enough rainfall occurred to clean module surfaces.
Valencia was the high-accumulation case. PM10 exposure persisted through several parts of the month, while limited rainfall meant the modelled soiling loss continued to rise.
Madrid shows a more moderate example. PM10 levels were lower than Valencia, and the modelled soiling loss increased more slowly, limiting the end-of-month impact.
Bordeaux provides the contrast. Particulate levels increased late in the month, but rainfall limited accumulation on uncleaned panels and kept the modelled soiling impact low.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Chinese TOPCon module prices fall as high-efficiency supply adds pressure - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
31 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Image: OPIS
The Chinese Module Marker (CMM), OPIS’ benchmark assessment for TOPCon modules below 645 W Free-On-Board (FOB) China, fell 0.91% this week to $0.109/W, with spot price indications ranging between $0.104/W and $0.119/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on July 28.
Sentiment for forward deliveries also weakened, with FOB China TOPCon module forward curve prices falling across the board. Forward prices for Q3 2026 and Q4 2026 loading cargoes fell 0.91% week-on-week to $0.109/W, while Q1 2027 loading cargoes declined 1.82% to $0.109/W. Q2 2027 and Q3 2027 cargoes both fell 0.92%, to $0.108/W and $0.109/W, respectively.
FOB China TOPCon mainstream modules weakened amid softer tradeable indications, as more supply of high-efficiency modules prompted manufacturers to lower offers and added pressure to the overall module market.
Price indications for high-efficiency TOPCon modules, defined as products above 650 W, were heard lower this week, at around high-$0.100/W to mid-$0.110/W on an FOB China basis. Meanwhile, back-contact (BC) modules command a premium of up to $0.02-0.03/W FOB over high-efficiency TOPCon modules.
The shift toward higher-efficiency modules has partly been driven by recent policy measures encouraging manufacturers to upgrade their product mix.
A national energy efficiency standard released in late June introduced a three-tier classification for crystalline silicon PV modules, effective Jan. 1, 2027. Under Grade 1, the minimum efficiency requirements for TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and BC modules are 24.0%, 23.8% and 24.2%, respectively. The corresponding minimum power output thresholds are 650 W for TOPCon, 645W for HJT and 655W for BC modules.
The policy push extended to pricing practices this week, with the China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIA) releasing the “General Principles for the Cost Accounting Model of the Photovoltaic Industry,” a new industry-wide standard that unifies cost calculation methodologies across polysilicon, wafers, cells and modules to provide a consistent basis for cost benchmarking.
The framework classifies manufacturing costs into cash cost, production cost and full cost, and requires vertically integrated producers to transfer products between manufacturing stages at the preceding stage’s full production cost, improving comparability with specialized manufacturers by preventing downstream costs from being understated. It also accommodates different technology routes, with CPIA planning to publish separate reference values for TOPCon, HJT and BC products.
CPIA Executive Secretary Liu Yiyang said the unified cost accounting model would enable prices to better reflect production costs, product quality and technological competitiveness, allowing efficient manufacturers to earn reasonable returns. Trina Solar Chairman Gao Jifan added that greater cost transparency could accelerate the phase-out of inefficient capacity, support more sustainable pricing and discourage excessive cost-cutting at the expense of product quality.
An industry source told OPIS that the framework’s impact will ultimately depend on its adoption in commercial negotiations, pricing practices and the transparency of cost disclosures.
Momentum behind the shift could build further, as market sources told OPIS that regulators are rumored to be considering an export tax rebate of up to 4% for Grade 1 high-efficiency cells and modules.
A source at a top-tier manufacturer said that, if confirmed, the rebate would significantly benefit high-efficiency products, with more competitive export pricing likely to incentivize buyers and encourage manufacturers to convert existing production lines toward higher-efficiency output. The producer added that the ongoing expansion into 650W modules would largely involve technical upgrades and retrofits of existing lines rather than construction of new facilities.
Another source at a top-10 manufacturer said lower-efficiency modules would face growing cost disadvantages if the export tax rebate framework shifts in favor of higher-efficiency products. title: New Zealand looks to legalize plug-in solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A solar regulatory review from New Zealand’s Ministry for Regulation suggests legalizing plug-in solar, approving installations under 10 kW by the next working day and allowing accredited installers to sign off on an installation less than 100 kW in size without an inspection.
Patrick Jowett
31 Jul 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Residential
Image: Wikimedia Commons, Microfotovoltaico
New Zealand’s Ministry for Regulation has recommended legalizing plug-in solar.
The recommendation forms part of a
solar regulatory review
review order
The report says that while demand for residential and business solar systems is increasing, potential uptakers are facing a time-consuming and frustrating customer journey due to the fragmented nature of existing regulations.
As a result, it suggests a series of changes to remove unnecessary barriers and improve how installation procedures work, in order to reduce installation delays, speed up approvals and remove disproportionate requirements.
Legalizing plug-in solar is one of fifteen recommendations which also includes exempting accredited installers from inspections for solar installations of up to 100 kW in capacity and requiring distributors to approve applications for solar installations under 10 kW by the next working day. For medium-sized installations under 100 kW, it suggests cutting approval times to under five working days.
The country’s regulation minister, David Seymour, says implementing the recommendations in the report would take the average installation approval for residential solar from around NZD 640 ($375.99) and three months to NZD 200 and six days.
Further estimates from the ministry indicate the recommendations could deliver net benefits of between NZD 28 million and NZD 50 million over ten years through lower compliance costs, reduced delays and the use of plug-in solar.
“The report recommends legalizing plug-in solar because there was no good reason for preventing Kiwis using it,” Seymour said. “Plug-in systems can be used by renters and people living in apartments who can’t access traditional rooftop solar. If they’re good enough for
, they’re good enough for us.”
New Zealand’s energy minister, Simeon Brown, has welcomed the proposals set out in the review.
“New Zealanders want more control over their power bills and want to harness the power of the sun,” Brown said. “These proposals will help give power back to the people by making solar uptake cheaper and faster.”
In April, New Zealand’s electricity authority introduced a
10 kW default export limit
for residential solar and battery systems in a move designed to standardize grid access.
New Zealand’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 836 MW at the end of last year, according to figures from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). Its largest solar farm to date, a
150 MW site
on the country’s north island, came online in July.

title: Study shows consequences of PV-related fires are generally limited in severity - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
An international study analyzed PV-related fires across the UK, Italy, Slovenia, and Sweden, showing that differences in reported fire rates are largely driven by national data collection methods and definitions. The researchers found that PV fires remain relatively rare, with data revealing that DC cables and connectors are the most common ignition sources.
Emiliano Bellini
31 Jul 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Image: Slovenian National Building and Civil Engineering Institute
An international research team led by the
Slovenian National Building and Civil Engineering Institute
(ZAG) has conducted an extensive review of all PV-related fires requiring firefighter intervention across the UK, Italy, Slovenia and Sweden and have found the diversity in results depends mostly on the respective reporting methodology.
“The harmonization of parameters and their terminology required in the reports that are filled by the firefighters after incidents would be extremely beneficial when thinking about cross-country comparisons,” corresponding author Nik Rus told
pv magazine
. “This would enable a much better comparison and also point out where the lacking safety levels might require prompter interventions.”
“Any regulations, building codes or fire safety requirements should definitely be data-based, especially given recent conflicting reports in the PV field,” he went on to say. “For instance, some safety components shut-off switches, which are theoretically designed and installed to improve the safety of PV systems, have, over the years, become one of the more common causes of failures that then evolve into ignition sources capable of leading to a fire. Such solutions not only harm the systems in which they are installed, but also distort the perception of broader efforts to improve the safety of PV systems.”
The study presents fire occurrence data across the four countries, with a detailed analysis of the Swedish dataset to identify ignition sources, fire development, and resulting consequences. “These data can serve as a foundation for risk analysis and risk management concerning rooftop PV systems, as well as provide general guidance for the fire safety of PV systems in general,” the scientists said.
They also explained they worked on national datasets that differ considerably in their definitions of PV-related fires. Italy and the UK primarily include incidents involving PV modules, whereas Slovenia and Sweden apply a broader definition that covers all PV system components, including cables and inverters. In order to bring clarity, the research team defined a PV-related fire as any incident involving a PV system component, regardless of whether the system initiated the fire or was affected after ignition elsewhere.
The Italian dataset, covering 2015–2024, shows an increasing number of reported incidents but cannot definitively determine fire origin. Most cases are classified as electrical or of undetermined cause, demonstrating the limitations of operational fire statistics for forensic analysis. Slovenian data became available after the introduction of a dedicated PV fire category in 2023, while Swedish data were further analysed through expert review to identify ignition sources and classify fire consequences.
The Swedish dataset provides detailed insight into damage severity, ranging from PV equipment damage to complete building fire involvement. UK statistics are based on keyword searches and may underestimate the true number of PV-related incidents due to narrower reporting criteria, the scientists said.
The analysis shows an overall increase in reported fires across all countries. When normalized by installed capacity or number of installations, the countries show comparable orders of magnitude, with Sweden and Italy displaying similar trends, the UK slightly lower values, and Slovenia higher values due to its broader reporting criteria.
Furthermore, the research team found that the Swedish dataset enabled a more detailed analysis of fire occurrence according to system size, ignition sources, and fire consequences. Fire frequency was found to vary considerably with system capacity, indicating that smaller systems generally have lower fire occurrence rates per installation but represent a substantial share of total incidents due to their large number. Larger systems showed higher variability because fewer installations result in greater statistical uncertainty.
Analysis of ignition sources in Sweden showed that DC cables and connectors were the most common origin of PV-related fires, accounting for approximately one-quarter of incidents. Other frequent ignition sources included DC switches and AC-side electrical central units. In contrast, PV modules and converters were less frequently identified as ignition sources, although annual variations remain significant due to the limited number of incidents.
The analysis also demonstrated that the consequences of PV-related fires were generally limited in severity. In Sweden, approximately two-thirds of incidents resulted only in damage to PV equipment, either indoors or outdoors. More severe events involving fire spread to adjacent surfaces accounted for around one-quarter of cases, while only a small proportion resulted in extensive building damage or total building loss. Most severe cases involved agricultural buildings or unoccupied structures rather than residential buildings.
“It should not be a surprise that some fires remain confined to the ignition source, others spread to nearby areas, and only some grow large enough to cause extensive damage,” Rus explained. “Our ongoing research examines the parameters that influence the early stages of fire development, assessing how the system limits or enables flame spread beyond the area of the ignition source.”
Overall, the findings demonstrate that PV-related fires remain relatively infrequent, but improved harmonised data collection and detailed analysis of ignition mechanisms are essential for effective risk management and future fire safety strategies.
“The reported numbers of fires per GW of installed capacity of PV systems range from about 5 to 13 annual fires for Italy, 7 to 19 annual fires per GW in Sweden, 2 to 4 fires per GW in the UK, and about 35 to 40 fires per GW in Slovenia,” the academics emphasized. “The numbers for annual fires per 100,000 systems are below 5 for the UK, between 14 and 24 in Italy, between 11 and 31 in Sweden, and about 80 in Slovenia.”
Their findings were presented in the study “
Fire Incidents Involving Photovoltaic Systems – An Analysis of Different National Statistics
,” published in the
Fire Safety Journal
. The research team included scientists from Sweden’s Bengt Dahlgren Fire Research, the Italian National Fire Brigade, and the University of Primorska in Slovenia.

title: This Smart Ring Tracks Glucose, Alcohol, and More Through Your Sweat
content:
Technology
In one half of the ring is housed the sensor array (orange stripes), the sweat extraction component, and the fluidic channel. Credit: David Baillot/UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering
A new smart ring could reveal far more than how well someone slept or how fast their heart is beating.
Engineers at the
University of California, San Diego
, have developed an experimental smart ring that continuously analyzes sweat from the finger to monitor several molecules associated with metabolism, nutrition, exercise, and alcohol consumption.
The prototype can measure up to four biomarkers at once, with interchangeable sensors designed to detect glucose, ketones, vitamin C, uric
, lactate, and alcohol.
The technology marks a shift from the physical measurements collected by most consumer wearables. Existing smart rings typically rely on signals such as heart rate, movement, and skin temperature, while the new device is designed to capture changing chemical information from inside the body.
“Commercial rings only provide biophysical information, but they lack molecular information about biochemical markers that offers deeper insights about an individual’s health status,” said study first author Tamoghna Saha, a postdoctoral researcher in Joseph Wang’s laboratory.
The biomarker monitoring ring next to a U.S. quarter for scale. Credit: David Baillot/UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering
The researchers describe the system in
Nature Communications
as the first fully integrated smart ring intended for routine biochemical monitoring. Wang is a professor in the Aiiso Yufeng Li Family Department of Chemical and Nano Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.
Collecting Sweat Without Exercise
One of the device’s most important features is that wearers do not need to exercise or deliberately work up a sweat. Fingers continually release small amounts of moisture, even when a person is resting. The ring captures that fluid through osmosis using a technique pioneered by Saha.
A soft material called an osmotic hydrogel creates a pressure difference that gently pulls sweat through the skin and into a narrow fluid channel. The process is painless and resembles the natural movement of water from soil toward the leaves of a plant.
The other half of the ring houses the flexible electronics, which consist of the battery and printed circuit board. Credit: David Baillot/UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering
Inside the ring, an electrochemical sensor array measures molecules in the collected sweat. The electronic signals are then converted into estimated concentrations using calibration factors developed for each wearer. This personalized calibration is important because sweat composition and the relationship between sweat and blood measurements can vary from one person to another.
Tracking Metabolism in Real Time
The ability to follow several molecules together may reveal patterns that a single reading would miss. Glucose and ketones, for example, provide different but connected information about how the body is obtaining and using energy. Continuous monitoring could show how those levels change after meals, during fasting, throughout exercise, or in response to medication.
“A ring capturing dynamic molecular information in real time would be extremely useful for making informed decisions regarding health, diet, and lifestyle,” said Wang. “For example, the ring’s ability to track both glucose and ketone continuously and simultaneously would greatly benefit optimal
dosing for the management of diabetes.”
In tests involving healthy volunteers and people with type 1 diabetes, glucose measurements from the ring closely followed readings from commercial continuous glucose monitors (CGMs). Its ketone results also closely matched measurements from commercial blood ketone meters.
A new smart ring continuously tracks multiple biomarkers at the same time, including glucose, ketones, vitamin C, uric acid, lactate, and alcohol. Credit: David Baillot/UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering
A Complete Lab on a Finger
The ring contains the entire sensing system rather than relying on a separate patch or external reader. One section houses the sweat collection system, fluid channel, and sensors, while another contains the battery and circuit board. Results are transmitted wirelessly to a smartphone app, allowing biomarker changes to be viewed over time.
A flexible, rechargeable zinc-silver oxide battery can power the prototype for up to 12 hours between charges. The circuit board is smaller than a U.S. quarter, and the outer shell is made from a 3D-printed polymer.
“Such integration onto the small footprint of a ring form factor is amazing,” Wang said.
Reference: “A fully integrated smart ring for daily biochemical monitoring” by Tamoghna Saha, Shichao Ding, Siyu Qin, Hannah Fishman, Rosie Pham, Te Gu, Muyang Lin, Yushan Xian, Barak Sabbagh, Abdulhameed Abdal, Gaoyuan Ji, Kittiya Sakdaphetsiri, Yi Fung Winsten Lam, Muhammad Inam Khan, Hao Luan, Zongnan Wang, Selene Tang, Omeed Djassemi, Samar Singh Sandhu, Sheng Xu and Joseph Wang, 23 July 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75980-z
This work was supported by the UC San Diego Center of Wearable Sensors (CWS) and the National Science Foundation – UC San Diego Materials Research Science and Engineering Center (DMR‑2011924).

title: Underwater Cave Bones Reveal Hidden Clues About Ancient Fossils
content:
Griffith University PhD Candidate Meg Walker examines retrieved megafauna fossils from Engelbrechts cave in Mount Gambier, South Australia. Credit: Steve Trewavas
Distinct marks on cave bones can reveal how underwater fossil deposits formed and changed over time.
Deep inside flooded caves, animal bones can remain remarkably intact for decades or even centuries. Yet researchers have lacked a reliable way to determine how the remains of extinct megafauna and other animals accumulated in these submerged sites or how the cave environment changed them over time.
Research led by
Griffith University
now provides a framework for reading those clues.
“By analyzing animal bones from two underwater cave systems in South Australia, we have revealed how different cave environments leave distinct preservation ‘fingerprints’ on skeletal remains,” said Meg Walker, a PhD Candidate supervised by Australian Research Center for Human Evolution Director Professor Julien Louys.
“Backed by radiocarbon-dated bones, we tracked how skeletons accumulated and were modified over decades and centuries in underwater caves, then compared them to those buried in dry caves. Using a range of methods, from the macro to the micro, we looked at features associated with wet and dry caves. Things like spatial distributions of the bones and their surfaces, down to elemental compositions and proteins trapped in ancient cells.”
The team dives Kilsby cave. Credit: Steve Trewavas
Underwater caves leave distinct fingerprints
The comparison showed that submerged caves can preserve bones with exceptional clarity, retaining both their overall form and fine surface details.
At the same time, the water left behind distinctive chemical and biological evidence shaped by available light and the organisms living in each part of the cave.
Near illuminated entrances, algae and aquatic plants grew in the cave water and sometimes directly across bone surfaces, producing recognizable traces.
PhD Meg Walker inside Engelbrechts cave. Credit: Steve Trewavas
Farther inside, in completely dark zones where sunlight and plant life were absent, the bones remained largely untouched.
Dry cave remains followed a different path. They lacked the aquatic signatures and instead showed damage from land-based bacteria and long grooves formed by growing plant roots.
Recent remains help explain megafauna
Walker and her colleagues worked with specialist divers from the Cave Divers Association of Australia to collect historical animal remains from Green Waterhole and Gouldens Sinkhole near Mount Gambier in South Australia.
The collection included native and introduced
such as kangaroos, emus, dingoes, possums, quolls, swamp rats, cows, sheep, pigs, and rabbits. Some of the remains may date to the first European settlement of the area during the 1840s.
Some of the fossil fragments have lain hidden on cave floors for thousands of years. Credit: Steve Trewavas
A framework for submerged fossils
“This study has delivered the first framework for interpreting how megafauna fossils formed, survived, and changed in underwater caves,” Miss Walker said.
“It will provide archaeologists and paleontologists worldwide with a powerful new tool for reconstructing past environments and histories in these challenging conditions.”
Reference: “Neotaphonomic characteristics of vertebrate site formation in underwater caves” by Meg M. Walker, Joanne E. Wilkinson, Mathew Stewart, Geraldine E. Jacobsen, Shwaron Kumar, Vladimir Levchenko, Stewart Fallon, Rebecca Esmay, Rachel Wood, Justyna J. Miszkiewicz, Gilbert J. Price, Elizabeth Reed, Joseph Monks and Julien Louys, 15 July 2026,
PLOS ONE
DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0343896
